title: HRW: donor cuts leave Rohingya children short of schooling
excerpt: Donor programmes enrol 312,000 of about 500,000 school-age Rohingya children, and the 2026 education appeal is still short, Human Rights Watch says.

image.alt: Shelters and latrines on a cut hillside in Balukhali Rohingya camp, Cox's Bazar
image.credit: S. Haiselden (VOA) / Wikimedia Commons, Public domain

content:
Donor-funded programmes in the Rohingya camps enrol 312,000 of roughly 500,000 school-age children, and about 90,000 more need a place this year because of population growth and new arrivals, Human Rights Watch (HRW) said on 16 November.

Education groups coordinated by UNICEF received $29 million of a $72 million request in 2025, HRW said. The 2026 request fell to $53 million, but donors had pledged only $36 million by mid-October. The United States funded half the Rohingya education budget before it stopped in 2025. Aid cuts closed learning centres for months in 2025, and officials warn they may close again.

Teachers described learning centres with no whiteboard, desks or benches, and three pupils sharing one set of textbooks. Classes run in two shifts a day. Funding cuts have also brought layoffs, a cancelled early education programme and less teacher training.

Rohingya-led schools

Community-led schools reach about 30,000 pupils but have no legal status, HRW said. The Examination Board of Rohingya Refugees, formed in 2025, oversees more than 125 of them. In October, Bangladesh let a few dozen Rohingya primary pupils sit an internationally recognised exam for the first time, with UNHCR support, and approved a Rohingya NGO's plan for a primary school for 240 pupils. No curriculum has been accredited, and the community schools cannot receive foreign funding directly.

"Donor governments have turned their backs on education for half a million Rohingya students," said Bill Van Esveld, associate children's rights director at HRW.

Why it matters

Education partners in Cox's Bazar had $36 million pledged against a $53 million request by mid-October, after a large shortfall in 2025. HRW is asking donors to fully fund education, Bangladesh to recognise the Rohingya-led school network, and humanitarian agencies to work with those schools. Out-of-school children are also more exposed to child labour and trafficking.

What to watch

  • Whether donors close the 2026 education gap before the year ends.
  • Any move by the government to accredit a curriculum or register community-led schools.

Sources

  • Bangladesh: Education Crisis for Rohingya Refugee Children, Human Rights Watch, 16 Nov 2026
